newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Irish bonds weaken ahead of EU ministers meeting.
newsitem.headline: Irish bonds weaken ahead of EU ministers meeting.

text.p: Irish bonds were weaker in thin late trade on Thursday in line with European markets as European Union finance ministers began meeting in Dublin, dealers said.
EU ministers are aiming to resolve outstanding issues over a budget accord that keeps deficits under control among countries joining a common currency.

The German-inspired stability pact has been one of the most contentious issues in the run-up to a single currency, with sharp differences over a strict definition of a recession seen as the main stumbling block.
"The market expects some progress to be made on the stability pact, but does not expect an agreement to be finalised," one dealer said.

By 1640 GMT, the 6.5 percent bond due 2001 had slipped 40 pence from Wednesday's close to 100.55 to yield 6.25 percent while the eight percent bond due 2006 had eased 55 pence to 107.40 to yield 6.80 percent.
"All markets in general are weaker today. There is no specific single reason for that," one dealer said.
"Ireland's inflation figure earlier today was marginally higher than had been expected but that is not particularly why the Irish market is weaker," the dealer added.

Irish inflation, as measured by the quarterly consumer price index, rose 1.9 percent in the year to mid-November compared with a 1.5 percent rise in the year to mid-August, the Central Statistics Office said on Thursday.

"I think the market is still shaken after the collapse in international markets at the end of last week which followed Greenspan's comments," the dealer said. "Add to this a bit of year-end profit-taking and uncertainty about the intentions of Japanese investors and it becomes easier to see why European markets, and Ireland in particular, have fallen," the dealer added. --Damien Lynch, Dublin newsroom 353-1-660-3377.
